message.content:
Below you’ll find a “tool‑box” of ways to pull **detailed interface data**—from simple one‑liner shell commands all the way up to programmatic access through SNMP/WMI/APIs. Pick the method(s) that fit your environment: | Platform | Tool / Command | What You Get | |----------|-----------------|--------------| | **Linux/macOS** | `ip -details link show `
or
`cat /sys/class/net//address && cat /proc/net/dev` | MTU, speed, duplex, flags, RX/TX counters, MAC, driver stats | | **Windows CMD** | `netsh interface ip show addresses ""`
`wmic nic where Name="" list full` | IPv4/IPv6 configs, DHCP state, MAC, adapter type | | **PowerShell** | `Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias ""`
`Get-CimInstance Win32_NetworkAdapter -Filter "NetConnectionID=''"` | Full IP stack + NIC properties | | **Cisco IOS/IOS-XE** | `show interface detail` | All hardware/software counters, errors, encapsulation, VLANs, QoS settings | | **Juniper Junos** | `show interfaces terse `
`show interfaces extensive ` | Same as above plus packet loss & traffic shaping details | | **Arista EOS** | `show interface description`
`show interface statistics ` | Interface description, bandwidth usage, error rates | | **SNMP** | OIDs such as `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.*` (`IF-MIB`) | Generic interface table – index, name, admin/status, operStatus, speed, mtu, mac, inbound/outbound octets/errors | | **RESTful API (e.g., Arista CloudVision)** | `/api/v1/interfaces/{id}` | Structured JSON payload with all metrics, health checks, configuration snapshots | --- ### Quick Start Guides #### 1️⃣ Linux – One‑Liner Detail Dump ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash IFS=':' read -r iface _ <<< "$1" # e.g., eth0 echo "=== $iface ===" printf "%-20s %s\n" "Name:" "$(basename $(readlink "/sys/class/net/$iface"))" printf "%-20s %s\n" "MAC:" "$(cat /sys/class/net/$iface/address)" printf "%-20s %s\n" "MTU:" "$(cat /sys/class/net/$iface/mtu)" printf "%-20s %s\n" "Speed:" "$(ethtool $iface | grep Speed | awk '{print $2}')" printf "%-20s %s\n" "Duplex:" "$(ethtool $iface | grep Duplex | awk '{print $2}')" echo "\n--- Counters ---" awk '$1 ~ /^$iface:/ {for(i=5;i<=NF;i++) printf("%s ", $i); print ""}' /proc/net/dev ``` Run: `./interface_detail.sh eth0` *Requires root privileges for some fields.* #### 2️⃣ Windows – PowerShell Snapshot ```powershell $int = Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object {$_.InterfaceAlias -eq "Ethernet"} $nic = Get-CimInstance Win32_NetworkAdapter -Filter "NetConnectionId='$($int.InterfaceAlias)'" [pscustomobject]@{ Alias = $int.InterfaceAlias Description = $nic.Description Status = $nic.NetEnabled ? "Up" : "Down" MAC = ($nic.MACAddress -replace ':', '-') LinkSpeedMbps = [math]::Round(($nic.Speed / 1MB), 2) IP = $int.IPAddress SubnetMask = $int.PrefixLength } ``` #### 3️⃣ Cisco IOS – Detailed View ```cisco Router# show interface GigabitEthernet0/1 switchport SwitchPort : Enabled Administrative Mode : Access Operational Mode : Down Access vlan : 10 Trunk native vlan : 99 ... ``` Add `detail` at end for extended counters: ```cisco Router# show interface GigabitEthernet0/1 detail GigabitEthernet0/1 is down, line protocol is down Hardware is iGbE, address is 00a0.c9ff.f001 (bia 00a0.c9ff.f001) Description: Uplink to Core Switch Internet Address is 192.168.100.1/24 MTU 1500 bytes, BW 100000 Kbit/sec, DLY 200 usec, ... RX packets 1234567 bytes 987654321 (938 MB) TX packets 7654321 bytes 876543210 (836 MB) ``` #### 4️⃣ SNMP Query Example (Python) ```python import pysnmp.hlapi as snmp def walk_if_table(community, host): iterator = snmp.nextCmd( snmp.SnmpEngine(), snmp.CommunityData(community), snmp.UdpTransportTarget((host, 161)), snmp.ContextData(), *[ snmp.ObjectType(snmp.ObjectIdentity('1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.'+str(x))) for x in range(1,8) # ifIndex, ifDescr, ifPhysAddress, ... ], lexicographicMode=False ) for errorIndication, errorStatus, _, varBinds in iterator: if errorIndication: raise RuntimeError(errorIndication) elif errorStatus: raise RuntimeError('%s at %s' % (errorStatus.prettyPrint(), errorIndex)) else: for varBind in varBinds: print(f'{varBind[0].prettyPrint()} = {varBind[1]}') walk_if_table('public', '192.168.1.1') ``` This pulls basic IF‑MIB attributes; extend the OIDs for more granular counters. --- ### When Do You Need Which Method? | Scenario | Recommended Approach | |---------|----------------------| | **Ad hoc check on a single machine** | Native CLI (`ip`, `ifconfig`, `netstat`, `get-net...`). | | **Automated inventory across many hosts** | Ansible playbook (`setup` module → `ansible_facts['interfaces']`), SaltStack grains, or custom script looping over SSH/SNMP. | | **Monitoring dashboards** | Exporters (Prometheus node_exporter, cAdvisor) feed into Grafana; or use vendor-specific telemetry (NETCONF/YANG, gRPC). | | **Device management platform integration** | Use the platform’s SDK/API (e.g., Arista ACI, Cisco DNA Center). | | **Legacy equipment without modern tooling** | SNMP walks or serial console logs. | --- ### Tips & Gotchas 1. **Permissions matter** – Many counters require elevated rights (root/admin). 2. **Link vs. Protocol State** – On switches, “down/down” means both physical and LACP/LAG states off; “up/up” indicates active link. 3. **Unit conversions** – Some utilities report kilobits per second while others use megabits; always double‑check units before comparing. 4. **Caching** – SNMP tables can change rapidly; consider polling intervals appropriate for your monitoring cadence. 5. **Security** – Never expose community strings or credentials publicly; prefer SNMPv3 or secure tunnels. Feel free to let me know what specific platform or toolset you're working with, and I can drill deeper into exact commands or scripts!
